newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.AFRICA DEC TRADE TO SIGNAL BETTER 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.AFRICA DEC TRADE TO SIGNAL BETTER 1997.

text.p: South Africa should have recorded a healthy trade surplus in December, paving the way to an improving trade balance in 1997, lead by higher exports, economists said on Friday.

The consensus forecast of analysts polled by Reuters was for a 760 million rand trade surplus in December, up from 378 million in November, although commentators cautioned the monthly figure was notoriously volatile.
The South African Revenue Services (SARS) gives only cumulative export and import figures for the year to date from which economists compute the monthly trade balance.
All analysts forecast a surplus for December with ideas ranging between 400 million rand and 1.3 billion.

BOE NatWest economist Nick Barnardt, at the top of the range, said he was upbeat on the December data. "I'm expecting a surplus of about 1.3 billion -- December is seasonallly a low import month," he said.
A SARS official said no firm date had yet been fixed for the release of December trade data, but it could be published as early as Monday.

South Africa's trade position has been improving in recent months as the sharp fall in the rand -- which tumbled 29 percent against the dollar in 1996 -- helps exports while a slowdown in the non-agricultural economy curbs imports.
However, economists said the full effects of the currency depreciation would only be felt in the trade balance in 1997.

"The positive impact of the depreciation on the export sector will only come through fully in 1997. At the same time, imports will be increasingly constrained following a fair amount of pre-emptive buying in 1996," said Hania Farhan, economist at ING Barings.
Farhan expects South Africa to record a trade surplus of $3.1 billion in 1997, up from $2.2 billion in 1996, which should help curb the country's current account deficit significantly in 1997.
Constantin Vayenas, emerging markets analyst at UBS in London, said on Thursday he expected the current account deficit to narrow to $1.6 billion in 1997 from $2.5 billion in 1996.

The Central Statistical Service said the December consumer price index, which many economists had expected to be released next week, would not be available until the last week of January due to delays in receiving all surveys.
December preliminary money supply data is also due in the week commencing January 27.
